title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth. The maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.

sample_test_cases.explanation: The longest path from the root to a leaf contains 3 nodes.

hints: The depth of an empty tree is 0.
The depth of a leaf node is 1.
The depth of a node depends on the depths of its left and right subtrees.
Use recursion to compute the maximum depth of each subtree.
explanation: For every node, the maximum depth is 1 plus the greater of the depths of its left and right subtrees. If the node is null, its depth is 0. Recursively compute the depth of the left and right children and return 1 + max(leftDepth, rightDepth). This DFS approach visits each node exactly once, resulting in O(n) time complexity and O(h) recursion stack space, where h is the height of the tree.

sample_test_cases.explanation: Both trees have the same structure and the same node values.

hints: Two null nodes are considered identical.

The current nodes must have the same value.
Recursively compare both left subtrees and both right subtrees.
explanation: Two binary trees are the same if they have identical structure and corresponding nodes contain the same values. Recursively compare the current nodes. title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values. Nodes at the same depth should be grouped together from left to right.

sample_test_cases.explanation: Nodes are visited level by level from top to bottom.

hints: Nodes at the same depth belong to the same level.
Process the tree level by level rather than node by node.
A queue is useful for Breadth-First Search (BFS).
Before processing a level, record how many nodes are currently in the queue.
explanation: Use Breadth-First Search (BFS) with a queue. Start by placing the root node in the queue. For each iteration, process all nodes currently in the queue, which represent one level of the tree. Collect their values into a list and add their children to the queue. After processing a level, add the collected values to the result. Continue until the queue becomes empty. This approach visits each node exactly once, resulting in O(n) time complexity.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid Binary Search Tree (BST). A BST is valid if for every node: all values in its left subtree are strictly less than the node's value, and all values in its right subtree are strictly greater than the node's value. Both left and right subtrees must also be valid BSTs.

sample_test_cases.explanation: Every node satisfies the Binary Search Tree property.

hints: Checking only the immediate children is not enough.
A node must satisfy constraints imposed by all of its ancestors.
Pass an allowable value range while traversing the tree.
Every node's value must lie strictly between its lower and upper bounds.
explanation: Use DFS while maintaining a valid range for each node. Initially, the root can take any value. For a node with value x, all nodes in its left subtree must be within (lowerBound, x), and all nodes in its right subtree must be within (x, upperBound). Recursively verify that every node satisfies its allowed range. If any node violates the range, the tree is not a valid BST. This approach correctly handles cases where violations occur deeper in the tree and runs in O(n) time.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree and two distinct nodes p and q present in the tree, return their Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA). The Lowest Common Ancestor is the lowest node in the tree that has both p and q as descendants (where a node can be a descendant of itself).
constraints: p and q exist in the tree

}

sample_test_cases.explanation: The lowest node having both 5 and 1 as descendants is 3.

hints: Think recursively.
What should happen if the current node is p or q?
Search for p and q in both left and right subtrees.
If one node is found in the left subtree and the other in the right subtree, the current node is the LCA.
explanation: Use a recursive DFS approach. If the current node is null, return null. If the current node matches p or q, return the current node. Recursively search the left and right subtrees. If both recursive calls return non-null values, it means p and q were found in different subtrees, making the current node their Lowest Common Ancestor. If only one side returns a non-null value, propagate that result upward. This algorithm visits each node once, resulting in O(n) time complexity and O(h) recursion stack space, where h is the height of the tree.

test_cases.note: Custom tree representation may contain hidden leaf arrangement.

hints: A valid path must start at the root and end at a leaf.
Keep track of the current path while traversing.
Subtract the current node's value from the remaining target.
When reaching a leaf node, check if the remaining target equals the leaf value.
explanation: Use Depth-First Search with backtracking. Maintain the current path and the remaining sum needed to reach targetSum. At each node, add the node's value to the current path and decrease the remaining sum. When a leaf node is reached, check whether the remaining sum equals the leaf's value. If it does, add a copy of the current path to the result. After exploring a node's children, remove the node from the current path before returning. This ensures correct path construction while exploring all root-to-leaf paths.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
description: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the right side of it. Return the values of the nodes you can see ordered from top to bottom.

sample_test_cases.explanation: From the right side, the visible nodes are 1, 3, and 4.

hints: Nodes are visible level by level.
At each depth, only one node contributes to the answer.
A BFS level-order traversal can identify the last node of every level.
Alternatively, a DFS that visits the right subtree first can record the first node seen at each depth.
explanation: Perform a level-order traversal using a queue. For each level, process all nodes currently in the queue and record the value of the last node processed. That node represents the rightmost visible node at that depth. Continue until all levels have been processed. Alternatively, a DFS that visits the right child before the left child can capture the first node encountered at each depth. Both approaches run in O(n) time.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
description: A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes is connected by an edge. A path may start and end at any node in the tree and must contain at least one node. Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum path sum of any path.

sample_test_cases.explanation: The maximum path is 2 -> 1 -> 3 with sum 6.

hints: The maximum path does not necessarily pass through the root.
For each node, consider the best contribution from the left and right subtrees.
Negative path sums can reduce the answer.
At every node, update a global maximum using leftGain + nodeValue + rightGain.
explanation: Use a postorder DFS traversal. For each node, calculate the maximum gain that can be contributed to its parent. The gain from a child is either the child's gain or 0 if the gain is negative. At every node, compute a candidate path sum consisting of leftGain + nodeValue + rightGain. This represents a path that passes through the current node and may terminate in both subtrees. Update the global maximum path sum with this value. Return nodeValue + max(leftGain, rightGain) to the parent because a parent can only extend one branch of the path. This approach visits every node once and runs in O(n) time.
